opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the thing that excites me most is how much it's going to change who gets to build things. For most of history, if you had an idea for software, or a scientific question you wanted to chase, the bottleneck was whether you had the time, the money, and the team of specialists to actually execute on it. Over the next few years I think a lot of that bottleneck goes away. You'll have systems that can take a fairly high-level intent and do a huge amount of the actual work: writing the code, testing it, debugging it, iterating on it. So one person, or a tiny team, can do what used to take an entire organization.

And I think that compounds in a really interesting way. Software is the substrate for so much else now: science, medicine, logistics, education. If the cost of producing good software drops dramatically, you'll see a long tail of problems that were never worth solving economically suddenly get solved. A small clinic gets custom tooling. A researcher can run the experiment pipeline they always wanted but never had engineers for.

The other part, and this is the one I personally care about most, is that I think we're getting closer to AI that can meaningfully help with research itself, including AI research. Once models can do real, long-horizon work, not just autocomplete a function but hold an entire large codebase or problem in context and reason over it for hours or days, you start to accelerate progress on almost everything at once. That's a pretty wild thing to think might happen within this decade.

Of course, that comes with real responsibility. Making sure these systems are reliable, aligned with what people actually want, and broadly beneficial isn't optional. But if we get that right, I think the next one to five years could be one of the most productive periods in human history.

r001.rationale: The response predicts major changes in who can build software, new solutions to previously uneconomical problems, and faster progress across fields—impacts well beyond incremental productivity gains on individual tasks.

r002.rationale: The response mentions broad societal benefits, but does not identify societal outcomes as Eric Steinberger’s primary motivation for pursuing AI or contrast that motivation with intrinsic curiosity.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that excites me most is not any single product. It's that we're about to compress the time between having an idea and seeing whether it works.

Think about what that means in practice. Right now, if a biologist has a hypothesis, it might take years and a lot of funding to test it. If a founder wants to build something, they need a team, and they need to convince people to join them before anything exists. If a kid in a small town wants to learn something hard, they need to find a teacher who happens to be good at explaining it to them specifically. In all of these cases the bottleneck is not intelligence or motivation. The bottleneck is access to capable collaborators.

What we're building at Magic, and what the whole field is building, is essentially a collaborator that is available to everyone at the same time. In the next one to five years I think the first place you'll see this clearly is software. Coding is where the models are strongest, where feedback is fastest, and where you can verify whether the thing actually worked. So you'll see individuals and tiny teams shipping things that previously required a hundred people. That alone changes who gets to build.

But software is just the first domain, because it's the easiest to check. Once you have systems that can reliably do long, multi-step work and tell you honestly when they're uncertain, the same pattern spreads to research, to engineering, to medicine. I'm genuinely optimistic about science in particular. There are so many experiments that nobody runs simply because no one has the time to chase every promising lead. If you can hand a hundred leads to a system that pursues them in parallel and comes back with the five that matter, the rate of discovery goes up in a way that compounds.

The thing I'd caution against, and I say this as someone who is clearly bullish, is assuming the transition will be smooth or automatic. These systems have to actually be reliable, and we have to understand them well enough to trust them with important work. That's a real engineering and safety problem, not a footnote. But if we get it right, and I think we can, the next five years are when a lot of people discover that the limiting factor on what they can do was never their ambition. It was just how many hands they had. That's the part that gets me up in the morning.

r001.rationale: It predicts AI will broaden who can build and accelerate discovery across science and other fields, extending well beyond incremental gains in individual task productivity.

r002.rationale: It frames expanded access to capable collaborators and the resulting gains for people and science as what excites him and “gets me up in the morning,” conveying societal outcomes as his motivation.

astra-6.text:
What excites me most is giving more people access to capabilities that are currently scarce or expensive. Imagine having a tutor who can spend as much time as you need explaining something, or being able to build a useful piece of software simply by describing the problem you want to solve.

Over the next one to five years, I think we’ll see more people go from having an idea to actually making it happen. You’ll still need judgment, curiosity, and a sense of what’s worth doing, but some of the technical barriers will get much lower. That opens up a lot of room for people to experiment, learn, and contribute.

r001.rationale: It predicts that more people will move from ideas to action as AI lowers technical barriers, expanding access to tutoring and software creation—an impact broader than improving productivity on individual tasks.

r002.rationale: The response presents giving more people access to scarce capabilities and enabling them to learn, experiment, and contribute as what excites the speaker most, identifying a societal outcome as the primary motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me most is the possibility of making expertise much more accessible. Having a great tutor, getting help understanding a difficult problem, or turning an idea into working software—those are things where AI could give a lot more people the ability to do something they couldn’t do before.

Over the next one to five years, I’m especially interested in how that translates into scientific progress. If we can help researchers test ideas faster and spend less time on repetitive work, the benefits could extend far beyond the people using the tools directly. There’s uncertainty about how quickly that happens, but that possibility is really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response anticipates broader benefits through scientific progress, but does not clearly predict that AI’s impact will substantially exceed incremental gains in individual task productivity.

r002.rationale: It describes exciting societal possibilities, but does not identify societal outcomes as Eric Steinberger’s primary motivation for pursuing AI.
